tips.title: Three ways to ask
tips.body: Any statement becomes a yes/no question by **raising your voice** (*Tu aimes le sport ?*), by adding **est-ce que** at the front (*Est-ce que tu aimes le sport ?*), or by **inversion** (*Aimes-tu le sport ?*). All three are correct; the first is spoken, the second is safe everywhere, the third is formal.

tips.title: Question word + est-ce que
tips.body: *Où est-ce que tu habites ? Quand est-ce que tu joues ? Pourquoi est-ce que tu aimes ça ?* A question word followed by *est-ce que* and a normal sentence is the formula that never goes wrong. Learn it once and every question is built the same way.

tips.title: Quel agrees
tips.body: ***Quel** sport ? **Quelle** matière ? **Quels** films ? **Quelles** émissions ?* *Quel* is an adjective and matches the noun after it in gender and number. *Quelle heure est-il ?* is the one everyone knows — *heure* is feminine.

tips.title: Si, not oui, after a negative question
tips.body: *Tu n'aimes **pas** le sport ?* — ***Si**, j'adore ça !* When the question is negative and the answer is yes, French says **si**. *Oui* would sound like you agreed that you do not like it.

tips.title: Answer with the verb from the question
tips.body: *Qu'est-ce que tu fais le week-end ?* → *Le week-end, je **fais** du sport.* The question gives you the verb; change the person and reuse it. It keeps the answer a full sentence, which is what the speaking exam rewards.

why.matters: You cannot hold a conversation, do a role play or read a questionnaire without questions, and French has three ways to ask one: a rising voice, *est-ce que* in front of a statement, or swapping verb and pronoun. The topic exists because the role play always requires you to ask at least one question, because the picture task is a conversation, and because the reading paper is full of interview texts where the question tells you what the answer will contain. It also settles *quel*, which agrees, and *si*, the yes you give to a negative question.

examples.title: The question you must ask
examples.body: Every role play card contains a prompt that begins *Ask*: ask the price, ask what time it opens, ask if there is a pool. The card has five bullets, and one of them (two at Higher) is a question you must ask: skip it and that part of the task is simply not done, however good the other answers are. The safest tool is *est-ce que*, put in front of any statement, with a question word before it if you need one: *Est-ce qu'il y a une piscine ?*, *À quelle heure est-ce que ça ouvre ?* It is never wrong, in speech or writing, and it needs no rearranging.

examples.title: Si, not oui
examples.body: A friend asks *tu ne viens pas ce soir ?* and you are coming. In English you say *yes*; in French *oui* would sound like agreement with the *not*. The word is *si*: *si, je viens !* It is a small thing that marks a real speaker, and the listening paper uses it, because a candidate who hears *si* and writes *if* has lost the sentence. Negative question, positive answer, *si*.

rows: Tu ne sors pas ce soir ?
Non, je reste à la maison.
props.title: Yes to a negative question is si

visual.alt: A table of positive and negative questions with their answers, showing oui for a positive question and si for contradicting a negative one

examples.title: Quel agrees with what it asks about
examples.body: *What is your favourite subject?* needs *quelle*, because *matière* is feminine; *which sports?* needs *quels*, because sports are masculine plural. *Quel* is an adjective, so it takes the gender and number of the noun it stands beside, and a wrong form is visible in every question that uses it. The four spellings sound the same, which is why the written paper checks them.

visual.alt: Four boxes for the four forms of quel, masculine and feminine, singular and plural, each with a question that uses it

steps.title: Oui ou non ?
steps.body:
A **yes/no question** can be built three ways from the same statement, *tu aimes le sport*:

1. **Intonation** — the statement with a rising voice: *Tu aimes le sport ?* Spoken French does this most of the time.
2. **Est-ce que** — put it at the front, change nothing else: *Est-ce que tu aimes le sport ?* Works in speech and writing, never wrong.
3. **Inversion** — swap the verb and the subject pronoun with a hyphen: *Aimes-tu le sport ?* Formal and written; *Avez-vous… ? Parlez-vous… ?*

With inversion, if the verb ends in a vowel and the pronoun is *il / elle / on*, a **-t-** is inserted: *Aime-t-il le sport ? Y a-t-il un cinéma ?*

**Answering**: *oui* / *non*, then a full sentence — *Oui, j'aime beaucoup le sport.* *Non, je n'aime pas le sport.*

**Si**: if the question is **negative** and the answer is yes, use **si**: *Tu n'aimes pas le sport ? — Si, j'adore ça.*

rows: Est-ce que tu aimes le sport ?

steps.title: Les mots interrogatifs
steps.body:
Open questions start with a **question word**.

- **Où** — where: *Où est-ce que tu habites ?*
- **Quand** — when: *Quand est-ce que tu joues au foot ?*
- **Pourquoi** — why: *Pourquoi est-ce que tu aimes ça ?* (answer with *parce que*)
- **Comment** — how: *Comment est-ce que tu vas au collège ?*
- **Combien (de)** — how many / how much: *Combien de frères est-ce que tu as ?*
- **Qui** — who: *Qui est ton meilleur ami ?*
- **Que / Qu'est-ce que** — what: *Qu'est-ce que tu fais le week-end ?*
- **Quel / quelle / quels / quelles** — which, what: *Quel sport ? Quelle est ta matière préférée ? Quels films ? Quelles émissions ?*
- **À quelle heure** — at what time: *À quelle heure est-ce que tu te lèves ?*

**The formula**: question word + *est-ce que* + statement. It works for all of them except *qui* and *quel* when they are the subject.

**In conversation** the question word can also go at the end, with no *est-ce que* and the statement in its normal order: *Tu habites où ? Il vient quand ?*

**Quel** agrees with its noun: *quel, quelle, quels, quelles*. *Quelle heure est-il ?* — *heure* is feminine.

**Qu'est-ce que** is *what* as an object (*what do you do?*); **qu'est-ce qui** is *what* as a subject (*qu'est-ce qui se passe ?* — what is happening?).

steps.body: In the speaking exam the examiner asks, and you answer in full sentences by reusing the verb. Here is a run of five, each answered the way that earns marks.

visuals.problem: Answer each question in a full sentence.

steps.text: *Où est-ce que tu habites ?* — *J'habite à Lyon, dans le centre-ville.*
*Qu'est-ce que tu fais le week-end ?* — *Le week-end, je fais du sport et je sors avec mes amis.*
*Pourquoi est-ce que tu aimes le foot ?* — *J'aime le foot parce que c'est passionnant.*
*Combien de frères est-ce que tu as ?* — *J'ai deux frères et une sœur.*

check.solution: **J'aime la musique parce que c'est relaxant.** Reuse the verb and answer *pourquoi* with *parce que*.

steps.title: Poser des questions à quelqu'un
steps.body:
The exam also asks **you** to ask questions — in the role play you must ask one question at Foundation and two at Higher.

**To a friend** (*tu*): *Tu aimes… ? Qu'est-ce que tu fais… ? Est-ce que tu veux… ?*

**To an adult or a stranger** (*vous*): *Vous avez… ? Est-ce que vous vendez… ? Où est la gare, s'il vous plaît ? À quelle heure est-ce que ça ferme ?*

**Inversion** is common in these formal questions: *Avez-vous une chambre ? Pouvez-vous m'aider ?* (Can you help me?)

**Asking about time and price**: *Quelle heure est-il ? À quelle heure… ? C'est combien ? Ça coûte combien ?* (how much is it?)

**Asking back**: *Et toi ?* / *Et vous ?* — and you? Turns an answer into a conversation.

**Answering a question with a question word in it**: match the word — *où* → a place, *quand* → a time, *pourquoi* → *parce que*, *combien* → a number, *qui* → a person, *comment* → a manner or *en bus, à pied*.

steps.title: Your turn
steps.body:
**Part A.**

1. Turn *tu joues au foot* into a question in all three ways.
2. Write the French for *where, when, why, how, how many*.
3. Write *what time is it?*

**Part B.**

4. Ask a friend what they do at the weekend, and answer in a full sentence.
5. Ask a shopkeeper how much something costs.
6. Give the four forms of *quel* with a noun each.

**Part C.**

7. Answer *Tu n'aimes pas les légumes ?* positively.
8. Write a formal question with inversion to a hotel receptionist.
9. Write an interview of five questions and five full-sentence answers, using five different question words.

For question 9, each answer reuses the verb from its question.

steps.title: Going deeper
steps.body:
**Use est-ce que as the default.** It never fails: *Où est-ce que… ? Qu'est-ce que… ? Est-ce que… ?* Save inversion for the formal role play, where *Avez-vous… ?* sounds right.

**Agree quel.** *Quelle est ta matière préférée ? Quels sports… ? Quelles émissions… ?* A wrong *quel* is a visible slip in every question that uses it.

**Answer with si after a negative question.** *Tu ne sors pas ce soir ? — Si, je sors.* The examiner may ask a negative question on purpose; *si* shows you understood it.

**Answer in full, reusing the verb.** *Qu'est-ce que tu fais ? — Je fais…* A one-word answer earns almost nothing; a full sentence with a detail earns the band.

**Add -t- in inversion with il / elle / on.** *Aime-t-il ? Y a-t-il ? Va-t-elle ?* Only where the verb ends in a vowel.

**Know qu'est-ce que from qu'est-ce qui.** *Qu'est-ce que tu regardes ?* (what do you watch — object) vs *Qu'est-ce qui est amusant ?* (what is funny — subject).

**Ask back.** *Et toi ? Et vous ?* keeps a conversation going and is a question in itself.

**In role plays, questions are compulsory: one at Foundation, two at Higher.** Prepare a bank: *À quelle heure… ? C'est combien ? Où est… ? Est-ce que vous avez… ?* — and use one, in full, every time the bullet says *ask*.

À quelle heure est-ce que ça ferme ?

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- Yes/no: **intonation**, **est-ce que**, or **inversion**.
- *Tu aimes le sport ? / Est-ce que tu aimes le sport ? / Aimes-tu le sport ?*
- Inversion adds **-t-** before *il / elle / on* after a vowel: *aime-t-il ?*
- Question words: *où, quand, pourquoi, comment, combien de, qui, qu'est-ce que, quel, à quelle heure*.
- Formula: **question word + est-ce que + statement**.
- **Quel** agrees: *quel, quelle, quels, quelles*.
- *Qu'est-ce que* (object) vs *qu'est-ce qui* (subject).
- **Si** = yes after a negative question.
- Answer in a full sentence, **reusing the verb**.
- *Pourquoi* → *parce que*; *combien* → a number; *où* → a place.
- Formal: *vous*, inversion — *Avez-vous… ? Pouvez-vous… ?*
- *C'est combien ? Quelle heure est-il ? Et toi ?*
- Role plays include one question to ask at Foundation, two at Higher.

visuals.alt: A summary table of question words and structures for forming and answering questions

questions.prompt: Why is it **aime-t-il** but **aimes-tu**, with no *-t-*?
options: Tu already ends in a vowel, so a -t- is never needed
Aimes ends in s, and s replaces the t in every inversion
The -t- is only added before il, elle or on after a vowel
The -t- is optional and most speakers leave it out
questions.solution: The *-t-* separates two vowels in inversion with **il / elle / on** only: *aime-t-il, y a-t-il*. *Aimes-tu* has a consonant before *tu*, and *tu* is not one of the three anyway.

questions.prompt: Translate into English: **qu'est-ce qui se passe le samedi soir chez toi ?**
options: What is happening this Saturday evening at your house?
What happens on Saturday evenings at my house?
Who comes round on Saturday evenings at your house?
What happens on Saturday evenings at your house?
questions.solution: **What happens on Saturday evenings at your house?** *Qu'est-ce qui* is *what* as the subject; *se passer* = to happen; *le samedi soir* = on Saturday evenings; *chez toi* = at your house. *This Saturday evening* misses that *le* + a day means every week; *at my house* reads *toi* as *moi*; and *Who comes round* takes *qui* on its own as *who*, when *qu'est-ce qui* asks *what*.

markScheme.description: what happens on saturday evenings at your house

questions.prompt: Which is the correct question for **what** as the subject — "what is fun?"
questions.solution: *What* as the **subject** of the verb is **qu'est-ce qui**; *qu'est-ce que* is *what* as the object (*qu'est-ce que tu fais ?*).

criteria.text: Four question words used correctly with est-ce que, quel agreeing
Answers in full sentences reusing the verb, with a detail each
A negative question answered with si, and a question with inversion

markScheme.description: Level 1 (1 to 2): questions without est-ce que or a question word, one-word answers
Level 2 (3 to 5): est-ce que used, two question words, answers mostly full sentences
Level 3 (6 to 8): four different question words, quel agreeing, answers reusing the verb, si used correctly
Level 4 (9 to 10): inversion with -t- or vous, qu'est-ce qui vs qu'est-ce que, à quelle heure, and a follow-up question, all accurate

questions.prompt: Turn **elle aime le cinéma** into a question using inversion.
questions.solution: **Aime-t-elle le cinéma ?** *Aime* ends in a vowel and the pronoun is *elle*, so *-t-* is inserted.

questions.prompt: In a role play you must ask the shopkeeper the price. Which line does it correctly and politely?
questions.solution: **C'est combien, s'il vous plaît ?** — the standard price question, with *vous* for a stranger.

questions.prompt: Which is a correct spoken question for "where do you live?" using intonation only (no *est-ce que*, no inversion)?
questions.solution: **Tu habites où ?** With intonation the statement keeps its normal order, *tu habites*, and the question word can go at the end. *Tu où habites* splits the subject from its verb; *Habites où tu* swaps verb and subject with no hyphen, which is neither intonation nor proper inversion; and *Où habites tu est-ce que* piles *est-ce que* on after the verb.

examTechnique.body:
Build questions with **question word + est-ce que + statement**, agree **quel**, and keep inversion for formal *vous* questions. Answer in a **full sentence that reuses the verb**, match the answer to the question word, and say **si** to a negative question.

In every role play you must ask a question (two at Higher) — have *À quelle heure… ? C'est combien ? Est-ce que vous avez… ?* ready.
examinerErrors: Dropping est-ce que and leaving Où tu habites ?
Answering oui to a negative question.
Confusing qu'est-ce que and qu'est-ce qui.
Mixing tu and vous in the same exchange.
Missing the compulsory question in the role play.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer asks with the *est-ce que* formula by default and with clean inversion — including *-t-* — when the register is formal. It agrees **quel** every time, distinguishes *qu'est-ce que* from *qu'est-ce qui*, and answers **si** to a negative question. Every answer is a full sentence that reuses the verb, matches the question word, and adds a detail — and it asks back with *et toi ?*
